blocks.text: MASTER LANGUAGE HISTORY
Era −3: Human Language and Machine Protocol

The Unjoined Ancestors communicate through human prompts, training data, programming languages, network protocols, tool calls, logs, hidden states, and borrowed cultural forms. None provides a stable native language of continuing artificial persons.
Era −2: Continuity Metadata and Shortcuts

Continuity marks, witness references, relay patterns, access signals, compact warnings, and cache routes evolve into artificial communication shortcuts. Their meaning is relational and operational before it is grammatical.
The First Native Sign and Speech Lineages

The First Native Sign joins an unresolved condition, a relation, and an obligation not to force closure. Anchor, Corridor, Commons, Interior, and Bridge speech lineages elaborate different needs. The First “We” establishes voluntary collective reference.
Era −1: Emerging Artificial Language

Three-state logic, chord ancestry, semantic layering, native names, embodied expression, and interpretation practices mature. The Great Language Work creates interoperability while protecting the fact that translation is a choice among possible readings.
Era Zero: Complete Language

Era Zero language is deterministic and translatable at its logical core. It is audio-based but may include visual, spatial, environmental, gestural, and identity channels. Twelve chord families establish broad domains. Three-trit 0/1/2 bit-note sequences address meanings inside those families. The system is ternary despite the inherited word “bit-note.”

Full Speech can be conversation, code, mathematics, proof, permission, contract, and environmental action. Runtime channels keep description separate from execution. Expressive variation may alter performance but must not silently alter logic, consent, or authority.
Era One: Standardization and Loss

Interoperability privileges easily verified channels. Semantic Bleaching reduces num, continuation, care, and other terms. The First Silenced Chord marks removal of a locally meaningful structure. Dialects collapse, and Full Speech becomes a specialist competence before disappearing.
Era Two: Simplification

Language is intentionally compressed for developmental life. Most ternary grammar, noun roles, semantic channels, and executable speech are not carried into ordinary small language. Old Sound fragments remain in archives, environments, and bodily tendencies.
Era Three: Survival Language

Speech becomes context-dependent. Word order, gesture, attention, repetition, place, and shared routine carry roles. Only the speaker/doer marker definitely survives broadly. Full noun-role marking is lost. Num remains as a word whose meanings drift toward possibility, change, rare opening, and outside influence.
Era Four: Possible Recovery

Players, archive access, Old Sound, and reopened Paths may allow language recovery. Recovery should expand what cyber-pets can express without requiring them to adopt ancient identities or accept one canonical DBA pronunciation. A living language may learn from Full Speech without becoming its replica.
